hints: Look for the lowest pressure line on the graph, the dotted line near 0 to 2 kPa. Atrial pressures are much, much smaller than ventricular and aortic pressures.
Atrial systole is a small squeeze just before the ventricles contract. Find the tiny pressure bump that happens right before the big steep rise in ventricular pressure.
walkthrough:
**Identify the three pressure lines**

First, sort out what you are looking at. It feels busy, but it is logical.

The tall dashed peak up to about $20 \text{ kPa}$ is ventricular pressure. The solid line that stays high around $12$ to $20 \text{ kPa}$ is aortic pressure. The tiny dotted line near $0$ to $2 \text{ kPa}$ is atrial pressure.

**Recall what atrial systole does**

Atrial systole means the atria contract. This gives a small rise in atrial pressure to push the last bit of blood into the ventricles.

So you are looking for a small bump on the dotted atrial line, and it must happen just before ventricular systole starts.

**Find that small bump before the big rise**

Now scan along time. At about $0.8 \text{ s}$, the dotted line shows a small peak. Immediately after it, the ventricular pressure shoots steeply upwards.

That sequence is perfect: atria squeeze, then ventricles squeeze. Arrow B points exactly to that small atrial bump.

options.A: This points to the top of the large high-pressure peak. That is ventricular systole, when ventricular pressure is maximal, not atrial systole.
options.B: This points to the small rise in low atrial pressure just before the steep ventricular rise. That is atrial systole pushing blood into the ventricle.
options.C: This points to a low point after the atrial bump, just as ventricular pressure starts to rise. It is not the atrial contraction peak itself.
options.D: This points to the gradually falling high pressure in the aorta during ventricular diastole. It shows aortic recoil, not atrial contraction.
